utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everyone present, the Ambassador, members of the Prosecution, the Defence, and the three accused. I have been informed that the other three accused are now ill. They'll be represented by their lawyers today, and as a result we can continue with the hearing today. I would like to point something out. It concerns the application of Rule 70. On a number of occasions yesterday there were some problems concerning the questions put. The Prosecution raised some objections. The witness himself objected. So I would like to remind everyone that if the witness believes that he shouldn't answer the question, he can tell us. If the representatives of the US government believe that the question doesn't fall within the scope of the examination, they can inform us of the fact. And similarly, if the Prosecution believes that the question is inappropriate, they should inform us. Unfortunately, the Judges are bound by this rule and the Tribunal's jurisprudence, so it's not just for the Chamber to decide. If the witness doesn't want to answer the question, the witness doesn't have to answer the question and I can't oblige the witness to answer such a question. Sometimes questions might be border-line questions; they might be in a grey area. Sometimes the matter might be very complicated. I do understand the situation we're in; however, I have to bear in mind the relevant Rule and the jurisprudence that has ensued as a result of the application of this Rule. We have until 1.45. I will now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Ambassador. My name is Vesna Alaburic, and I am a lawyer from Zagreb, and I represent General Milivoj Petkovic in these proceedings. You've mentioned the good terms you were on and your cooperation with the Croatian government, with representatives of the political opposition. You said that you were at Budisa's -- at the convention of Budisa's liberals. You also mentioned the independent media organisations who were involved in the protection of human rights. As we are familiar with you and your activities in Zagreb, would you agree that the USA was the most active country when it came to dealing with a series of political issues in Croatia, and through their activities, they strove to contribute to the development of democratic social relationships.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly that would be true from 1993 through the end of my tenure, and I'm not saying that isn't true beyond. I just will confine my remarks to that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you often hear many people assess the situation in Croatia, people from the independent and dependent media, an assessment according to which you attributed to the protection of human rights in the Republic of Croatia, an assessment that without your activities the situation in Croatia would have been far more serious, far worse?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate the implication of your question, but I think that is really for others to say and not for me to say. I certainly hope it is true that the United States and I personally did contribute to an improvement in the situation in Croatia, both in terms of peace, development of democracy, and protection of human rights of all the communities without with regard to ethnicity. But I suppose that final verdict should be made by others.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Over the last few days you told us that you went to Croatia at the invitation of President Tudjman, among other things, and also that representatives of governments from other republics of the former Yugoslavia wanted the USA to become involved in an active way in resolving the crisis in the former Yugoslavia. I'd like to remind you of an interview of yours, an interview you gave to the magazine Globus.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show us the interview on the screen. 4D00326 is the number of the interview in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There are only two passages from this interview that I'm interested in for the purposes of the question I want to put to you, but if you believe that other parts of the interview are of interest, we can translate them, too. So I've only had these two passages translated and I'll quote what you said. "Besides, we did not simply decide to come here. We were asked to come, we were begged to come. I can't tell you how many times President Tudjman asked for the help of the United States in 1993, 1994, and 1995. He asked us to get involved, to become diplomatically engaged, and to send our soldiers over here. We have heard the same sort of things from leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as that is concerned, we received the same requests from President Milosevic." Do you remember this interview, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did many interviews, so I can't say that I specifically remember this one, but now that you show it to me, I -- I mean, I do remember it and I'm a hundred per cent sure that the words that are spoken here are mine. It certainly reflected -- reflects my thinking then and now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, when I look at the document in B/C/S that I have before me, I can see that a question must have been first put. It's in bold. And then there is the answer. Here you have shown us the Ambassador's answer, but it would be interesting to know what the journalist's question was. Do you have the question? Could you inform us of the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are referring to the B/C/S version, could we have the next page on the screen, the next page of this interview. That's right. The question starts at the beginning of the first column, and it is as follows: "Would it be correct to say that the Croatian state, because of the decision of the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina to boycott the elections, has now found itself in the most difficult political and international situation to date and that they are seriously threatened with the imposition of sanctions?" The beginning of the answer is as follows, and I quote: "The friends of Croatia were, in any event, very disappointed by the step that the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina threatened to take. The USA clearly stated our concern, and the European Union did so, too. I believe that perhaps the leaders in Croatia and Bosnia and the leaders among Bosnian Croats have failed to understand what is at stake, and I must say that this shows a very poor understanding of international relations." And then there is an explanation that concerns the billions of dollars that the USA had spent to secure peace in Bosnia. And then another passage follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary to continue. The text on the screen is an answer to a question that was posed, and you have now mentioned the question. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to what you yourself said, as early as 1993, Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman, desired that the USA become actively involved in resolving the crisis in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So my question is: On the basis of your conversations with the late President Tudjman, could one say that he believed that the American army and administration were effective, or was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did think we were effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did he sincerely believe that by engaging the USA it would be possible to put an end to hostilities and that it would be possible to secure peace?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he felt that our engagement was the last chance for bringing an end to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience, if someone wants to use military means to obtain a political objective, would it be possible for such a person to request that the USA become militarily involved to deal with the problems in the territory? If President Tudjman wanted to take or conquer part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would he have asked the American army to come to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I can put it in a simple way, too.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about two different time periods here. At the time that we sent our troops in, of course, it was following the Dayton Peace Agreements, and there was no thought, as best I can recall, expressed to me by President Tudjman, about the engagement of US troops prior to the peace agreement because he understood, as did everybody else, that that was not going to happen. And so the involvement of American troops really was something that occurred with the Dayton Peace Agreement. He very much wanted them to come to eastern Slavonia as part of the Erdut Agreement, but that was not going to happen with the US administration. So instead we sent an American general to be the head of the UN mission, who is also a diplomat, Jacques Klein. So the issue of US involvement, frankly, was the diplomatic power of the United States, and that was what he was seeking, the active diplomatic engagement. Perhaps it's useful to recall that when the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia in 1991, the approach of the Europeans was that this was a European problem and Europe would handle it, and that the United States didn't need to get involved. And that, of course, was something that very much fit the views of the Bush administration, which had just come out of the Persian Gulf War and was dealing with all the issues related to the collapse of the Soviet Union, and then, of course, a presidential election in 1992. I think in 1992 the Croatian government, and certainly the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did want to see a more active US involvement, but it was an election year and that was not going to happen. And so the hope was in 1993, with the new administration, that it would happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. As far as the policies of the EU are concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. If I have understood you correctly, your country became involved or started to become involved as of the time that you presented your letter of accreditation, or did that happen, in fact, before you actually arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly began before I arrived. We did have a special envoy for the former Yugoslavia, but I think it's fair to say that through 1993 and then in 199 -- well, through 1993 and continuing in 1994 and 1995, our involvement increased very dramatically. Even from the start there was some minimal US involvement, but it wasn't what the parties in the region, at least the Croatian and Bosnian governments, would have liked to have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. We will deal with EU policies and US policies in the second part of my cross-examination, but I'd like to clarify something with regard to the engagement of the US military in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Would you agree with the statement that there was a discussion in the international community about the authority of the UN forces or the mandate of the UN forces that were to be sent to the territory of the former Yugoslavia? I'm referring to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was always discussion in the international community about the authority or mandate of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the most hotly debated issue the question as to whether these forces would have the right to intervene in armed conflicts? Or would they just have the right to escort humanitarian convoys and monitor the situation with regard to these convoys in the field?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many discussions about what the rules of engagement would be for the UN forces -- UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that UNPROFOR did not have the right to intervene in armed clashes and to actively try to put an end to such clashes because members of the American army were not part of UNPROFOR and because the American army was not present in the field?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with that statement. That was not the reason why UNPROFOR did not have the authority to intervene in armed conflict. There were many militarily capable forces, extremely capable forces, including from France and Great Britain. And the reason they didn't intervene had to do with the mandate of those -- of the UNPROFOR mission as well as the decisions of the troop-contributing countries. I don't think that had anything to do with the absence of US military.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that President Tudjman suggested that NATO forces become engaged in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly that was true following the Dayton Peace Agreement. NATO took the role in the -- took the lead role in the international force. And prior to that I guess there was discussion on his part of a NATO role.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, before NATO became involved and before the USA became involved, how many years prior to that date did President Tudjman first request that NATO become involved in trying to secure peace in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to turn to the subject of the late President Tudjman, because I believe that your opinion of President Tudjman is of great importance for this case. On the first day of your testimony you told us that the late President Tudjman believed that Bosnia and Herzegovina wouldn't and shouldn't survive as a sovereign and independent state, and you said that on numerous occasions he exposed his views on territorial boundaries and on his territorial aspirations with regard to part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question is: Would it be correct to say that the Government of Republic of Croatia didn't carry out an attack on the neighbouring country of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or rather, the Army of the Republic of Croatia didn't carry out such an attack?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was started by Milosevic and his Bosnian Serb allies, but the Army of the Republic of Croatia was in fact involved in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including fighting the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but that's not an answer to my question. I was talking about the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me help you when it comes to defining the term of "aggression". The Prosecution, in its indictment, hasn't charged the accused with being involved in an aggression, nor do they claim that Croatia carried out an act of aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm talking about aggression in the usual sense of that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but this is getting into legalese and legal terminology. And so there's no misunderstanding and so the Prosecution's position is not misrepresented, it is indeed the Prosecution position that the Government of Croatia was involved in active aggression against the Bosnian government and sent its troops into Bosnia to do just that. So I don't want the Prosecution position or the indictment to be misinterpreted, whatever terminology one wants to use.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the legal problem is concerned, I don't believe it's just a matter of the legal concept of aggression. The witness has spoken about legal armies, legal governments, et cetera. So I don't believe that my question is a question that the Ambassador can't understand and answer. As far as referring to the contents of the indictment is concerned, I don't think it's necessary to enter into a dispute right now. But there is something that is illogical. One cannot help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rephrase your question clearly so that the Ambassador, who has studied law, can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question was: Could you confirm that the Republic of Croatia was never involved in an aggression against its neighbouring country Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct, of course, that I have a legal degree, but I perhaps should point out that I've never practiced law. And I'm reluctant to get drawn into offering a legal opinion, not because I'm shy about offering my opinions, which I think those who know me know that I am not, but I'm in a courtroom full of very qualified lawyers, and it strikes me that there are other people who are better able to come to these conclusions. I'm really here to testify as to facts about my experience as a diplomat in Croatia. So if I could -- I'll just try to state the facts as we saw them. The Croatian army -- I hope I can answer this, because the Croatian army was involved in military action against the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We considered that illegal. We, as I have testified, raised this repeatedly with the Government of Croatia, and we ultimately -- not ultimately, but we regularly -- we threatened sanctions on Croatia, including being part of an ultimatum on the 3rd of March, 1994, by the President of the Security Council, which gave Croatia two weeks to withdraw its troops from Bosnia. And that was because we thought the activities were illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ambassador, in very simple terms, the question put to you by the Defence has to do with the term "aggression." In diplomatic language, the aggression of country A against country B is what, exactly? Is it a war at a particular point in time, in the course of the life of two countries? What does it mean when one talks about the aggression of one country against another?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but, again, there is a specific term of legal art --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I don't appreciate your intervention. I put a question to the witness in diplomatic terms. He's a diplomat, and as a diplomat I asked him how he understands the term "aggression". Without referring to Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, I asked the witness how he interpreted the term "aggression," if one is speaking about the aggression of one country against another. He can either answer the question or not. Let him try and answer it. If he doesn't want to answer the question, he won't answer the question. Ambassador, answer the question if you like; and if you don't want to, we'll move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Avoiding, then, a legal term, but how did we diplomatically understand "aggression" or how would I understand it? First, of course, a military attack on one country on to the territory of another in circumstances where there was no case of self-defense; and second, I would include in that sending in troops from one country on to the territory of another country against the will of the lawfully -- of the internationally recognised government of that country, and I would certainly include in that situation circumstances where the troops of the foreign country were fighting against the forces of the lawfully constituted government of the country. So those would all fit within what I would define as aggression, in a diplomatic sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be interesting to see to what extent, according to this definition of aggression, the USA has committed aggression. So please tell me, apart from the wars that are common knowledge, on how many countries has the USA perpetrated aggression, and how many aggressions is it perpetrating right now? If you cannot answer that question, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's beyond the scope. Move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A few words about the attitude of the late President Tudjman towards the international community. To the best of your knowledge, was President Tudjman aware that without the blessing of the international community, the Republic of Croatia would not become an independent and sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was the late President Tudjman aware that without the blessing of the international community no changes in the borders of the countries of the former Yugoslavia would be possible unless all the sides involved agreed otherwise?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question has a kind of -- has a double -- maybe it's not exactly a double negative to it, but it's a little hard for me to answer, the way you've posed it. You ask: Was President Tudjman aware that without the blessing of the international community no changes in the borders of the countries of the former Yugoslavia would be possible? That's really kind -- one question. I mean, do you mean that, even without the blessing of the international community, as long as all sides agreed, it would be possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll put the question in two parts. So the first part of the question is: Was President Tudjman aware that without the permission of the international community there could be no changes in the borders of the countries of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he knew that without the acceptance by the international community there would be no internationally recognised changes in the borders of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will clarify the second part of my question. For example, if the Republic of Croatia, according to a constitutional procedure, decided to cede part of its territory to, let's say, Montenegro, would that be a problem between those two countries? But we'll move on because my time is running out. Tell us, please, to the best of your knowledge, was President Tudjman aware that without the agreement of the international community there could be no changes in the internal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how it would have been possible to change the internal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time without the blessing of the international community?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for one thing, he sponsored the creation of the Republic of -- so-called Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which the international community did not condone. That republic consisted -- continued long after it was supposed to have been dissolved. Documents continued to refer to it long after it was supposed to have been dissolved. And in spite of demarches by the United States, the European Union, and others, that this was an illegal entity and in violation of treaties, if he kept it going. So I guess the answer to the question -- that's why I say I don't agree with your statement. And that's just one example. I can offer another. The creation of the Republika Srpska was something that was opposed by the international community, and yet it took place in 1992 -- or the -- self-styled at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I may draw this conclusion: Your answer confirms my thesis, because without the blessing of the international community, no changes occurring in the internal order of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be recognised. But let's take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. Your question was: Could there be changes in the internal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina without the recognition of the international community? My answer is: Yes, there could be and there were many changes. Of course, now you modify that to say: Well, there weren't internationally recognised changes. Well, that's, of course, a truism, but there were in fact changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm only concluding that those changes could not have been recognised without the blessing of the international community, which means in fact that the blessing of the international community was a prerequisite for changes of the internal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that statement at all because you could have changes that were not recognised, and in fact there were many changes that were not recognised. I also frankly disagree with the use of the word "blessing." Sometimes one has to recognise some things that one does not bless at all, in fact, some things that one finds distasteful but can also be a reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's approach it from a different direction. Would you agree that in late 1992 or early 1993, when the conflict began -- I apologise, not 1993, but at the time of the break-up of Yugoslavia and the creation of the independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was Bosnia-Herzegovina a unitary state?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to have to observe that you're asking me questions that really go beyond the scope of what I'm here to testify to, not that I could not answer that question. But, frankly, I wonder why you're asking me. I mean, this is -- this is a -- it really is beyond the scope of what I'm here to deal with. It's a simple question, but I wonder why you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll be very happy, Mr. Ambassador, to explain the reason for my question. The Serbian and Croatian entities and the forms of organisation of the Serbian and Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina is something you have labelled as illegitimate and illegal. So the question is: What kind of order would it be in which Republika Srpska was something illegal? I want to explain what kind of state Bosnia-Herzegovina was in order to explain how Republika Srpska and Herceg-Bosna were created. I want to discuss the legitimacy of the so-called government in Sarajevo. Therefore, I believe my question is directly connected to your responses over the past two days, because, according to the opinion of many, the essence of the war in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina was an attempt to reach an agreement about the internal order. The Muslims wanted a unitary state, whereas the Serbs and the Croats, each in their own way, wanted a complex state, consisting of three national entities. That's why I'm putting these questions. So, to the best of your knowledge, at the time of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, was Bosnia-Herzegovina a unitary state?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour. Excuse me, Ambassador. I'm going to endorse -- the Ambassador may want to answer the question, but I'm going to endorse his earlier objection. I think this is beyond the scope of the Rule 70 permission and outside the scope of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ambassador, the Prosecutor believes the question put by the Defence might fall under Rule 70, but it's for you to decide whether you should answer the question. The question put by Ms. Alaburic is in fact very complicated, but I'll summarise her question. What she wants to know is your opinion, the opinion of a diplomat or a representative of the US government in Croatia, your opinion as an ordinary citizen. She would like to know whether, in your opinion, the creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which was described as illegal, is in fact illegal, since the Defence is trying to support the thesis according to which Bosnia and Herzegovina was consisted of three entities, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims. So that is the gist of her question. Answer it or don't answer. If you don't want to answer it, we'll move on to another matter. It's as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that explanation. And thank you to Defence counsel for the explanation. And I will answer the question within the scope of my testimony -- within the scope of what I'm -- of Rule 70. And so I will take the question to be about how the United States viewed Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time that I was Ambassador, and the answer is that we viewed Bosnia and Herzegovina -- well, let me answer and if you don't like my answer you can follow up, because I think I'll get to the point -- I'll get to the point that you're after.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but my question does not refer to the time when you became Ambassador but 1990 and 1991, when the former Yugoslavia broke up.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me answer it in this way: In 1993, when I arrived -- when I arrived in Zagreb and we examined these questions, we considered the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina that came into being following the referendum in 1992 to be an internationally recognised state with the constitutional -- legal constitutional structure that it had and that the government, headed by President Alija Izetbegovic, was the lawful government of the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that other entities, including the so-called Republika Srpska and the so-called Herceg-Bosna, were not lawful entities. And that was our view as we saw it in 1993 of the events in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have on e-court P08632. This is David Owen's book "Balkan Odyssey." It's page 51 and 52 in Croatian; in the English text, pages 41 and 42. Excuse me, we only have the English text, and I'll correct the page number. It's pages 51 and 52 of the book. It's pages 41 and 42 in e-court. Pages 51 and 52 of the book and electronic pages 41. Can we zoom in a little bit? Yes, if we could zoom in to page 51, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, could you read the first sentence of the last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In all our conference papers and meetings, however, we were scrupulous in treating Izetbegovic as president and his ministers as members of the government of an independent state, while being aware that they constituted one of the three parties to a dispute which had to have a negotiated solution."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now turn the page, page 52 of the book, which is page 42 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the last three sentences of the first paragraph. The last three sentences of the first paragraph. The sentence I'm interested in begins with the words "The collective Presidency as a democratic body ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up a bit, please? Raise it a little -- scroll up -- or rather, scroll down. I'm sorry, scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph which -- the sentence begins with the words, "The collective Presidency ..." Could you read from there until the end of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The collective Presidency as a democratic body with meaningful representation from the three constituent nations was, by the autumn of 1993, no longer a reality. The real decisions were made elsewhere. We were, in effect, dealing with a Muslim government for a predominantly Muslim population."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you feel that Mr. David Owen is correct when putting forward these standpoints on who Alija Izetbegovic was representing?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the United States was concerned, President Alija Izetbegovic was at president of the entire country of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was the head of state of an internationally recognised nation, recognised by the United States, and a member of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when you spoke to the representatives of all three constituent peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who did you speak to as the representative of the Serbs of the Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I can explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just give us the names, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer is: I was Ambassador to Croatia. I didn't speak to any of the representatives of the Bosnian Serbs in the period of time that is the subject of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know who, as the representative of the Bosnian Serbs, participated in meetings organised by representatives of the international community relating to relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us who at these meetings attended as the representatives of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it depends on which one, but sometimes it was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at these meetings did the Bosnian Muslims have their representatives?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the internationally recognised state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, President Alija Izetbegovic, was at many of these meetings. It is incidentally quite normal in circumstances where there is a conflict that the president of the country might also meet with -- as part of peace negotiations, with leaders of armed groups within a country. That does not in any way make him solely the representative of one party. But it is also true that a political leader, a president, is quite often both the president of the entire country and the leader of one party. For example, George Bush is both the President of the United States and the leader of the Republican Party in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, if Alija Izetbegovic represented all three constituent peoples making up the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it follows that the Muslims did not have their representative at these meetings. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that President Alija Izetbegovic was the president of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the -- that covered the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I also said that he was the leader of a political party, and so, as is quite normal, he might participate in discussions, basically wearing both hats. Again, if President Bush, as the leader of the Republican Party, is sitting down with Democratic congressional leaders, he's in some sense doing that in both capacities; he's the national -- the elected national leader and he is the leader of his party with a political agenda negotiating with the opposite party.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In view of this dual role you are describing, please tell us whether Mr. Izetbegovic, before he spoke, stated whether he was speaking as a representative of the Muslims or whether he was speaking on behalf of the entire state, including the Serbs and Croats? How did you know when he was speaking as a representative of the state and when he was speaking as a representative of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, could we have some dates and places on this? Which meeting -- which meeting are we talking about? We can't talk about five years of history all in one go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, are there any specific meetings you have in mind with regard to which the witness could be of use to us? Because right now we don't really see where you're going -- we can't really see where you're going.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am thinking of the meetings in Geneva, New York, Washington, and Dayton, all the places at which there was discussion under the auspices of the international community of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As the witness has stated that he knew who the representatives of the individual nations were at international meetings, the witness himself might tell us what meetings he was referring to. This is a very important question. If a country such as the USA treats one side as the legitimate government representing all three sides, then serious questions arise as to the role of the USA in the events which ensued. But we will clarify this, if it's relevant to clarify at what meetings Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was representing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the problem is that the Judges don't have to deal with the role of the USA. That is not a matter dealt with in the indictment. We don't have deal with this role within the conflict. We have to deal with acts of certain individuals with regard to a criminal enterprise, a joint criminal enterprise, with regard to crimes committed in certain municipalities. And now you want to discuss the role of the USA in this matter. Historically it might be of interest, but with regard to the defence of your client and with regard to the judgement that we, the Judges, have to render, we might be wasting our time. It's a matter of strategy. Put a question to the witness, a direct question. Say: In my opinion, I believe such and such; do you agree with me or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour. I thought by -- that by showing David Owen's statement about Alija Izetbegovic being the president of the Muslims, of only one side in the conflict, I believe that we were dealing with the merits. As far as relevance is concerned, I think this question is relevant in order to be able to assess this witness's testimony. So if we can know on what basis he assessed the situation in the former Yugoslavia. That's why I think these questions are important.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as your testimony is concerned or your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could you tell me how much time I have used up, since my colleagues are looking at the clock and wondering how long they have been waiting for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The microphone wasn't on. The registrar has just told me that you have used up 42 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I'd like to move on to the subject of the illegal status of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On a number of occasions yesterday you told us that the army of the Bosnian Herzegovinian Croats, that was called the HVO, was an illegal body. I have a few questions about this, if we can be very brief. Would you agree with me if I said that while the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was in existence, the JNA was the only legal army in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the territory of the other republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the situation was more complicated because there was both the JNA and there were Territorial Defence forces that were set up pursuant to the constitution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But the Territorial Defence forces, if you can remember the constitution, weren't in fact part of the army. There was only one army and that was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the issue really has to do with what are lawful armed forces, whatever you call them. But ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you answer my question: Is it true to say that the JNA was the only legal army at the time of the existence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say that the JNA was the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that there is no doubt about the fact that in April 1993, Bosnia and Herzegovina -- in April 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state; that means that the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia didn't exist in 1992. Would you agree that at that time and before the JNA openly sided with the Serbs, both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at that time, at the beginning of 1992, there was no army in existence in Bosnia and Herzegovina that could have been considered as a legal army, in accordance with your criteria, an army that could have provided security for the population and the property of that territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would say is that it was for the lawful Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the internationally recognised Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to establish whatever type of armed forces it wished to have, and that armed forces would be the lawful armed force or armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your answer, I can come to the conclusion that the Sarajevo government didn't act in this way. My following question, then, is, if we may make a digression, my question is: At the time of the French Revolution in 1789, which army was in fact the legal army?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't share -- I do not accept that you can come to the conclusion that the -- from my answer that the Sarajevo government did not act -- did or did not act in any way. That is not a fair or legitimate inference from what I said. And second, I will absolutely say that the French Revolution is beyond the scope of Rule 70 and I will refuse to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you agree with me if I said that at the time of a revolution, when a state is breaking up, when new states are being established, the concept of what is legal and what is not legal, what is illegal -- well, these aren't concepts that are easy to define. What is legal -- well, what is legitimate is something that hasn't been covered by any provisions, by any rules, up until that point in time, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Let me repeat, then. Madam Alaburic, I believe that your questions, although they are partly based on historical facts and legal considerations, we are really rather far from the present issue, that is why Ambassador came here to be listened to. And that's why I believe it would be better if you would ask questions from him which are related to the case before us and which are under Rule 70. I would appreciate if you would be so kind to follow this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I said that I would just make a brief historical digression and then return to Bosnia-Herzegovina to say that at the beginning of 1992 Bosnia and Herzegovina didn't have an army that would defend the inhabitants from attacks launched by the Bosnian Serbs. So the question, then, is: Does each people, does the population given territory, have the right to self-defense? Do they have the natural right to organise themselves, to defend their homes, to defend their property from attacks that they are subjected to?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there certainly is a right that people have of self-defense in some circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that under the leadership and command of the HVO, Mostar was in fact liberated from Bosnian Serb forces? And not just Mostar, in fact, as the accused have added, this was not only the case in Mostar but in many other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, could you be more specific? Which exact date do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June 1992, the liberation of Mostar under the command of the HVO, Muslim units under the command of the HVO participated in the liberation of Mostar as well as many Muslims who were among the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you regard such an act as an illegal act?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When implementing the Washington Agreement, did Generals Rasim Delic, on behalf of the ABiH, and Ante Roso, on behalf of the HVO, participate on a totally equal basis when it came to resolving military issues?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that these two generals signed a document on accepting principles for the structuring of a federal army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that ABiH and the HVO became parts of that federal army, fully equal parts or fully equal components of that army?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is correct, and of course that would be pursuant to, you know, the decision of the lawful government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I now have to put another question to you. When concluding these agreements, did representatives of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Croats participate, Mr. Zubak, and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic on behalf of the Muslims; and there were certain other officials from the Sarajevo government who were involved in other agreements. Did they participate on a fully equal basis?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately I have many other questions, but maybe I could just refer to them for the sake of the transcript. I wanted to ask the witness about his statement that President Tudjman was the spokesperson for the Herzegovina Croats -- Bosnia-Herzegovina Croats in a certain way. I wanted to analyse the acts of the embassies of Bosnia-Herzegovina who promoted Muslim interests alone. Then I wanted to ask questions about the possibility of exerting influence by Tudjman, Susak, and Granic on the Bosnian and Herzegovinian Croats. I wanted to analyse the concept of Croatian territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which doesn't mean the territory of the Republic of Croatia, it means the territory of the Croats who lived in that area. And then I wanted to show that it wasn't only Tudjman who was interested in maps; everyone was interested in maps. All those who participated in discussions on the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina were interested in maps. I also wanted to discuss how Mr. Tudjman presented his views on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina to everyone that he spoke to, and it wasn't necessary to have a secret service or a special source of information to find out what his opinions were. I think this is very important when it comes to trying to establish criminal enterprise. I wanted to analyse the witness's statements about Muslim state, the fact that it was Tudjman's desire to have a Muslim state. David Owen's book, "Balkan Odyssey," contradicts this, as well as the Izetbegovic-Krajisnik agreement, according to which, after two years, it would be possible to organise a referendum on separating from Bosnia and Herzegovina. All of this took place in September 1993. I wanted to prove that the Muslims were in favour of war. This was established by a British delegation when they visited the field. I wanted to prove that there were no plans for evacuation, and that in a communication of the witness he spoke about the information that he received from BritBat, according to which Croats had been organised to leave parts of Bugojno, whereas the Muslims wanted to present this as an evacuation alone. And I wanted to analyse the relationship between the US policies and the policies of the EU. And finally -- I apologise. And finally, I wanted to show how people who participated on behalf of the USA in establishing and implementing the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Agreement believed that US policies in Bosnia and Herzegovina were very questionable. I wanted to prove that Republika Srpska is now facing a referendum or is about to have a referendum on independence today, and the same discussions are being held about the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I wanted to conclude with the words of Lord Owen, who said that the USA, when it changed its policies after Bill Clinton came to power, if the USA hadn't got involved in that way in 1993, in February 1993, the Vance-Owen Plan would have been accepted and peace would have been obtained in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps some of the other lawyers will put some of the questions that you didn't have the time to put to the witness and your desires will be fulfilled. We have ten minutes before the break. It would perhaps be best to have a 20-minute break now and then resume. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, just an intervention because I'm not next. I want to know, if Ms. Alaburic took one hour and 20 minutes and I'm making -- I'm being very firm about this one, because I've been attacked in the past of using everybody else's time. I think when we have a gentleman on the witness stand, or a lady on the witness stand, who absolutely must leave on a particular date, on the last day of their testimony, we need to respect each other's time. And I don't think we can take -- we have to recalculate the hours, because now if you are coming in last, you end up with no time. At the same time, I want to voice my concerns that the time constraints, unfortunately, place many of the Defence lawyers in a position where they cannot adequately defend the positions or their clients. Ms. Alaburic made her record on that. So while I support her efforts, at the same time I'm not here to condone some other Defence team taking my time in defending my client, because I'm not part of a joint criminal enterprise. I'm here representing one client and one client only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have ten minutes before the break. It would be best to have the break now and resume afterwards. We'll resume in 20 minutes, about 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll resume. Yes, Ms. Alaburic, what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have one request, since my colleague Karnavas has complained because I have used up more time granted to me and this is prejudicial to him, I'd be grateful if the registrar can inform us of the exact amount of time I have taken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. 57 minutes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic now has 45 minutes, Mr. Prlic 45 minutes, and Mr. Coric 25 minutes. I'll now give the floor to the first Defence team. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Coric's Defence has no questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So now it's either Mr. Stojic's Defence team or Mr. Prlic's Defence team. It's as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it was -- I was going to go first and then Mr. Murphy was going to follow me. I guess I don't want to pass up the point that I was trying to make earlier. On the last day of a witness, I think we need to re-calibrate our accounting system, because intervention -- unless we're going to have the witness fly back from the United States if we run out of time, and I don't think that's going to be the case or should it -- or is it fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As you can see, it's not easy being a Defence lawyer around here. First, let me begin by saying that I was somewhat pre-empted by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have to react to what you said. When you said that it's not easy to be a Defence lawyer here, you're putting the Tribunal into question, and this is not permissible. This is not something that a Defence lawyer may be allowed to do. You can say that you're working under very difficult conditions, that there are time restrictions, but we are all aware of the fact. But you cannot attack the Tribunal by saying that it is not easy to work as a Defence lawyer here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't attacking the Tribunal, I meant even among ourselves, as colleagues, times are -- at times we are at conflict with each other. That's what I meant, Your Honour. No offence towards the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me say that I was somewhat pre-empted by Mr. Scott yesterday when he asked you whether you were here to help the Prosecution. I wanted to, first of all, publicly extend an apology on that. I thought I overstated the position. I thought you were trying to be helpful, and I certainly want to apologise if I -- by making that remark. But having said that, it would appear, at least from listening to your testimony, that you are quite proud of your achievements and in fact you are somewhat of an advocate of the Clinton administration's policies towards Tudjman and your involvement in Croatia as an Ambassador on behalf of the United States. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job as an Ambassador was to be an advocate of the United States and of the president whom I represented. And I think, looking back, the United States did accomplish a lot. I think we played a very important role in bringing an end to the Muslim-Croat war, to alleviating the suffering, and to bringing an end to the war in Bosnia, and to bringing a final peace agreement with the Erdut Agreement in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you would agree with me, even as you stand here today, you're advocating those positions as being correct positions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here telling you the truth as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to step back a little bit prior to your arrival. Looking at your resume and your career, I think it's safe to say that you are for your entire -- I mean from the time that you finished university, you spent your career in foreign affairs, international affairs, call it what you will, but in that field basically. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you -- but you -- prior to your appointment as Ambassador to Croatia, you were not part of the diplomatic corps in the sense of being -- rising through the ranks of the State Department?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I was on the staff of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so that would mean you being appointed Ambassador to Croatia, that would be a political appointment?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Not that the other appointments aren't, but there's a slight difference between someone rising through the State Department and someone who is a political appointee. Now, in light of your previous experience, it would appear that you either had what I would call a rabbi, somebody pushing you in order to make -- get Clinton to -- President Clinton to put your name to the senate, or you raised a bunch of money for him - and I don't think that's the case - or perhaps you even were in the wings assisting the Clinton campaign during the campaign period with perhaps position papers on foreign policy issues. Am I correct in any of the three?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the term "political appointee" implies somebody who either raised money or, you know, was a former elected official. And I was a -- I had spent my career as a government employee. I certainly was not chosen because I raised any money, because I didn't raise any money, and I was not chosen because I wrote position papers for the campaign, because I was not involved in a significant way in the campaign. Certainly there were people, both inside the administration and, not surprisingly, in the US Senate, who knew me and thought that I had some skills and could make a contribution to the administration. But I guess the answer is that almost immediately after the election, I was called by the transition team perhaps before any -- anybody would have intervened and asked if I was interested in joining the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it at that time, sir -- I have to remind myself to speak slower. But was it at that time when you were contacted that you were told that Croatia was the possibility or the former Yugoslavia was the possibility, in light of your prior experience with the region?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time. In fact, a number of positions were discussed with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you did say that you did not -- you were not involved in a significant way. So I guess the question might be: Well, to what extent were you involved? If not significant, to what extent were you involved in the campaign process as far as helping Clinton on foreign policy issues as the campaign was waging?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I knew the people -- many of the people who were advising the campaign, so from time to time I would talk to them. But, as I said to you, I think there was no -- I mean, I can't really remember any particular involvement except for some conversations. It's possible I might have written somebody a note. In 1992 I was travelling a very large amount. I think I made 12 different international trips in that year alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there's a reason why I'm asking these questions and it might become obvious at some point. But, as I understand it, your primary focus dealt with the Kurdish issue in Iraq. I mean, not that you were not involved in other issues. But at least both on a professional and on a personal level, it would appear that if you do have one real, real specialty, it's in that area.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, if you would have asked people in 1992, probably they would have said that my specialty was South Asia, India and Pakistan. But I certainly achieved a fair amount of recognition for the work I had done on Iraq, and on Kurdistan in particular, in the period 1987 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And at that point in time, as today - and I don't think your views varied that much - it would appear that your solution for Iraq sort of to have it split up to three different nations - the Kurds, the Sunnis and the Shiites - I'm oversimplifying it, of course, but for all intents and purposes, that's sort of your position. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, my position is that Iraq has already split up into an independent Kurdistan and an evolving Shiite entity in the south, a Sunni region in the centre, and that the United States and the international community should not engage in what would be a very costly and probably futile effort to put it back together again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I would call it social engineering. You would agree with me that at least - and I don't want to get too involved into this discussion - that the Sunni and the Shiite are not constituent nations as you would have, for instance, in Bosnia, where you had Serbs, Muslims and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the Kurds are a nation. But I write in my book, "The End of Iraq," that the Shiites -- there is an element of the Iraqi Shiites that is -- of course it is a religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as the Bosnian -- as the Muslims in Bosnia were as a religion. But it is a religion that has elements of a national identity. It's evolving. And so, in fact, there are some parallels, and I write about this, between this Shiite identity and the Bosnian Muslim identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, by the time that you got appointed and hit the ground in Zagreb, you were sort of -- you arrived sort of in the middle of the third act of a four-act play. I mean, if you look at the dissolution of Yugoslavia as act one; you know, act two is the war with Slovenia, Croatia, and their independence; act three, the situation in Bosnia up until the Washington Agreement; act four, Washington to Dayton. I'm simplifying it, but basically, for all intents and purposes, you arrived in the middle. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it depends on how many acts you think there are in this play, since Montenegro just became independent a few months ago. But I arrived as Ambassador after the break-up of -- after the independence of Croatia and Slovenia and after the independence of Bosnia and the start of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during the campaign, the 1992 campaign, presidential campaign, of the United States, this issue, as I recall, was sort of hotly debated, or at least debated, between the Bush folks and the Clinton folks, with Clinton saying that if he got elected he would be much more active and much more engaging and perhaps even advocating, maybe not directly but indirectly, the possibility of the use of troops there to solve the situation. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He advocated -- he certainly advocated a more active American role. He advocated the use of air-strike -- air power against the forces that were attacking Sarajevo. He advocated lifting the arms embargo. I do not think he advocated sending American troops into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. He wasn't advocating it outrightly, but basically the tone was that they wanted a much more robust - I think that's the term that is used in diplomacy often - a much more robust approach to this issue?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He felt that we should not allow the indiscriminate shelling of civilians in Sarajevo or the death camps. But I don't want to leave you with the impression that the sending of American ground troops into Bosnia was in any way contemplated, either directly or indirectly, because it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But the use of force was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Air power, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. And air power can be just as deadly, if not more deadly, than, say, use of troops. I think we saw that later on.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of air power in Bosnia, when it finally took place, was very significant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that, if we look at the flip side of the coin, the criticism during the campaign of the Bush folks was that they were -- that they were not doing enough in this conflict, because, as you put it, it was viewed at that point in time as a European problem, not an American problem. Let the Europeans deal with it; they could handle it, and so on and so forth. And I'm, again, oversimplifying it, but that was the message, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were multiple reasons. It wasn't that the Bush administration's attitude was: Let the Europeans handle it. It was that the Europeans said: We can handle it. 1992 is the year of Europe. And the Bush administration, which, to be fair, had its hands full with the break-up of the Soviet Union, the aftermath of the first Persian Gulf War, and with an election which was turning on dissatisfaction -- on the sense that the president had not done much on domestic issues and was too engaged in foreign affairs, the last thing it wanted to undertake was this new problem in the former Yugoslavia. And I might also add that some of the top advisors to the first President Bush, notably Deputy Secretary of State, Lawrence Eagleburger, and National Security Advisor, Fred Scrowcroft, had been involved in Yugoslavia diplomatically and so they had a certain bias on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say bias. Well, Eagleburger, as I understand it, at one point in time had been the Ambassador to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so he would be, as one might say, sort of an old hand -- an old Balkan hand. And if I'm not mistaken, Zimmerman worked under him at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, he worked under him when he was Deputy Secretary of State. I don't recall whether Zimmerman was a political officer in Belgrade when Eagleburger was Ambassador, but that might be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nonetheless, Eagleburger was fairly familiar with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Clinton administration takes over in January 1992; correct? 1992.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, January 20th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, 1993. Now, by this point in time, you had this ongoing process, negotiating process, that had started with the Europeans in trying to find a solution to the break-up of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us yesterday that before coming over here, coming over to the region and taking up your post, that you had been briefed. And as I recall your testimony yesterday, you said by the time you even arrived, you had sort of your marching orders - and I'm using that term, you didn't, but basically that's what it was - that you had your marching orders to do a couple of things. One was to inform Tudjman that he had to change his policies towards Bosnia and Herzegovina; and number two, he had to get rid of two people in particular - one was General Praljak and the other was Mate Boban. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to make clear, I did say that I had been briefed and talked to many people in preparation for taking up my assignment as Ambassador to Croatia; that, of course, is normal. I also had the experience of having made four trips from 1991, 1992, to the former Yugoslavia as it was breaking up and having met all the leaders, almost all of them. The instructions that I had certainly involved raising the humanitarian issues, access for convoys, the things I testified to yesterday. But it was my conclusion, after a period of time of being there on the ground, that Boban and Praljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had to go.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- had to go, and that was a decision that was supported by my government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I might add that much of the focus was on Boban, since he was the top leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So just to make sure that I'm absolutely clear, before you came to Croatia, you had not formed an opinion as to whether Boban and Praljak should go.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I had not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any information about those two individuals? Or was it when you arrived and you began to, you know, make the rounds, as it were, and formulate your opinion, you know, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is, of course, hard --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- 13 years later, to remember what information I got and when. The kinds of briefings that are prepared are very extensive and the conversations I had were very extensive. But I think it's -- I think it's fair to say that Boban and Praljak had come up in the course of the briefings before I went out, but it -- you know, it would be hard for me to pin-point a day or a place because it's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what about with respect to President Tudjman and his policy towards BiH with respect to, you know, what you've testified to, the use of HV soldiers in Croatia or humanitarian aid? Was that something that you had been briefed on in Washington and there had been a fixed position, you know, with you, you know, upon arrival to give a stern lecture, message, to Tudjman as to what you knew and what you expected of him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's an impression that instructions are kind of a written piece of paper that you follow, and that isn't -- that isn't the way the process works. But what it was that the leaders of the Clinton administration wanted me to do was to bring pressure to bear on to President Tudjman to respect the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to end the atrocities that were being committed by Bosnian Croat forces, to end the Muslim-Croat war, to play a constructive role in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Bosnia peace process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But from your answer, I think I can work backwards and draw the conclusion that at least the Clinton administration, whoever they were and whoever was briefing you or instructing you - I suspect it might have been the Balkan Desk in the State Department - but by that point in time, at least the Clinton administration had a fixed opinion that Tudjman was doing all these things in Bosnia and Herzegovina, hence, you know, your mission or part of your mission. Correct? In other words, what I'm trying to say is: You didn't arrive, see what was happening, and say: Oh, by the way, troops are going there; humanitarian aid is being blocked; atrocities are occurring. You were being told this before you arrived and you had somewhat of a fixed opinion based on the information that you had before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's leave out the notion of a fixed opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but to stay with the notion that we knew about these things before I arrived. Yes. We had an embassy in Zagreb. There was a lot of reporting about this. There was reporting in the press, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the Clinton -- if I can go back a little bit further -- and incidentally, have you read David Owen's book? It was mentioned before by my colleague. I suspect you have an interest in the area. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you probably flipped to the back to see where your name is mentioned and gone in to see where you were mentioned anywhere? Well, you can answer the question without looking at the Prosecutor. I mean, that is a normal reaction.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I looked in the index to see if I was mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It might not fit within Rule 70. Okay. Now, in this book -- and I think you would agree with me that Lord Owen is a serious individual.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that he is a serious individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by the time that he took up his post, if we are to take him at his word, he had been an MP for about 24 years, and during that career period, he was also Foreign Minister for Britain or the United Kingdom; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in his capacity during that period, he was not there as an individual or representing the British government, but rather he was there on behalf of the EU. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And along with him, his counterpart, his sidekick, as it were, was Cyrus Vance, who, as you well know, was one of the wise men of Washington?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be inaccurate to character Cyrus Vance as David Owen's sidekick. In fact, in that partnership Cyrus Vance was the senior figure, and, as I understand it, from having talked to Vance, it was Vance who helped get Owen appointed as the EU representative, because Vance had known Owen from the time when Vance was Secretary of State and Owen, Foreign Secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Mr. Vance was there on behalf of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not on behalf of the State Department?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. He was the UN representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
