utterances.text: But as some of us know, he had served as the Secretary of State on the Carter administration; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until he resigned --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As a result of what happened in Iran --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and disputes with Brizinski, as I understand it. But before that, before the Carter administration, he had served in some capacity, I can't remember whether it was the Johnson administration or maybe even earlier.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had served in the Johnson administration, maybe the Kennedy administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you would look at David Owen's book, it would appear that the Clinton administration, when it got elected and when it took over in January, almost from the very outset, it was dead against the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is David Owen's view. Frankly, I don't think it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Owen, for instance, characterised a meeting in January of 1993 where he and Vance - and there was a reason I called him sidekick and you absolutely were correct in correcting me, because I wanted that admission that he was actually the point man - and here is Mr. Vance with Mr. Owen and they're meeting your boss, which would have been Christopher, Warren Christopher, the then Secretary of State, where they're trying to brief him on the Vance-Owen Plan. And it would appear, at least if we are to take Mr. Owen at his word - and we may have him here to testify - that Mr. Christopher was totally uninformed. This is in January. And the -- you're --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggest that the question about what Mr. Christopher knew or didn't know might be directed to Mr. Christopher. I can't speak to what Mr. Christopher knew or didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And also Mr. Owen points out where -- after that meeting, where it was rather obvious to them that Mr. Christopher was not -- not only was he uninformed but also didn't seem to give -- pay much attention to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, slightly thereafter they're passing some cameras and then later on they're watching on CNN where Christopher is giving a news conference, a briefing, where he is, in essence, disrepresenting the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall reading that -- I do not recall that part of the book, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as I said, I read parts of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then there are other parts of the book, and we'll introduce it at some other point. I don't have enough time. But I'm just giving you the big picture here, where Mr. Owen - and this was brought up by my colleague a little bit - paints a picture where, at least in the early stages of the Clinton administration, January, February, March - the Clinton administration is doing everything it possibly can to kill the Vance-Owen Peace Plan because, in their terms - and this is widely publicised in the media - that it is promoting ethnic cleansing. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an extremely complicated matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Stick with me on just the press. Was it coming out in the press? Was the Clinton administration using its relations, it's public relation resources -- and, you know, we know how articles can be planted; people can write -- that happens. The Bush administration has taken it to the extreme. But, I mean, do you recall following the press during that period, as you're getting ready to take up your post, where the Clinton administration is outright coming out and saying, through the press, that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan is actually promoting ethnic cleansing? And the reason I'm mentioning this is that one of the parties, the Muslims, are going to have to sign on to this. And if the Clinton administration is making these -- these statements publicly, obviously the Muslims are not going to go along. So do you recall this being -- happening in the press? Yes, no, maybe, or I can't recall?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I don't want to press you on this, but if you -- if it's in David Owen's book, and assuming that he gives us references, would you have any reason to disbelieve him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Owen also states in his book that the Vance -- that throughout this peace process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I would like to tell you that the French booth cannot follow you. Please kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, would you agree or disagree or would you take exception to Mr. Owen's characterisation in his book where he says that, in his capacity as EU representative, along with Mr. Vance, who was -- the two of them were the architects of this peace plan, members of the European community, such as France, Germany, Denmark, and others, were fully behind the peace plan that they were promoting at the time. And so they weren't -- he and Vance were not acting as individuals, but rather they were collectively getting assurances from the representative countries that the plan itself, what they were promoting or what they had -- and pushing at the negotiating table, was a plan that was acceptable to the Europeans?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm very sensitive to the issue of time. I know Mr. Karnavas has limited time, but I still feel that I must indicate here, I think we have to get some specifics as to passages of the book, that the book can be put in front of the witness. I just cannot honestly say -- I don't know if we're talking about Mr. Owen's characterisation of his book or Mr. Karnavas's characterisation of his book. And these are -- as the Ambassador said, these are very, very specific items. We don't know the context of particular passages, and I think particular passages should be put before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be delighted to do that. I simply do not have the time. I am -- and one would have to take me at my word, because at some point we are going to be introducing the book. And if I'm mischaracterising the evidence, then obviously not only do you disregard what I say, but also -- and incidentally, it is -- it's a Prosecution exhibit, it's P08632. So it's not as if I'm quoting from a document that is unbeknownst to the Prosecution. It's their document. I'm using their evidence. And I suspect Mr. Scott has read the book himself. If not Mr. Scott, Mr. Mundis for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't dispute, Your Honour, that the Prosecution has the book. That's not the issue. The issue is putting the passages in front of this witness so this witness can make fair response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour. I'll rephrase the question

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware, or did you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, the Judges trust the lawyers who are making such references, because, according to the Rules, the lawyers shouldn't misrepresent matters. If Mr. Karnavas is referring to something, it means he has read it -- it should mean he has read it. Unless the Prosecution immediately says that the Defence is saying something different, it shouldn't be a problem. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I am misquoting, then I can be sanctioned as well. But I appreciate the Court's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, if he's misquoting because I have no passage in front of me. We're talking about a long book, so how do I know whether Mr. Karnavas is taking something out of context or mischaracterising it or not? We have no passage in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, if I was in your place, I'd have the book in front of me, and when Mr. Karnavas intervenes I'd follow. You're contesting what he says but on what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, number one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, but you're accusing him of misrepresenting the truth. This is a Prosecution exhibit. He has given you the number. You can just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know what passage he is talking about. Which page and paragraph number would you like me to turn to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour, just to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, to the extent that it's possible, refer to the page or paragraph, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this is the problem. I don't want to spend the time, but there is a whole chapter, it's chapter 3, "Vance-Owen Peace Plan." I don't know what part of this chapter the Prosecution has not read, but it covers it in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you, sir: Did you read that chapter of the book by any chance? Yes, no, maybe, or I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Do you recall whether -- do you know whether the European countries that were involved in this process, whether they had signed on to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, whether they were in agreement of this plan?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were generally supportive, but I couldn't speak to it in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would it surprise you, sir, that during this period, during this negotiating period, that every side pulled out maps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it one thing that you might recall from reading the book, that Mr. Owen was of a fixed opinion - and you made some references to this - that he was of a fixed opinion that borders were not sacrosanct, that maybe there was room to negotiate with respect to the borders of the various republics?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be clear about that so that there's no conclusion. The Vance-Owen Plan did not involve changes in the international borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I want to -- one thing follows another --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I want to go step by step. I will be very fair with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have already said that David Owen did favour changes in the international borders, but that that was his view and it was not shared by the United States government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, and I think we're in total agreement, okay? But what I am suggesting to you is, before you come on the scene with the US plan, there are these discussions with individuals such as Lord Owen and his interlocutors, such as Tudjman, where he is advancing ideas, maybe not ideas that the US likes and will have to deal with later on, but nonetheless he's already talk -- they're talking about changing of borders even at the international level. I'm not suggesting that this is being promoted, but there are discussions.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not part of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're a lawyer and you've testified in front of the Senate. I'm just a Defence lawyer. You're highly experienced. Surely I'm no match for you. But you know my question. Could you answer it? You don't need to re-read the question.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were having these discussions -- Owen was discussing changing international borders with the folks, such as Tudjman, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've testified that he discussed some limited changes, such as a corridor in which territory north of the Sava, north of Brcko, would be ceded to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But my question is --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- ceded to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, my question is more precise, because this is what I'm trying to get at: You've come here and told us that Tudjman - and I agree with you on this - that Tudjman would pull out these maps, and whoever he saw, especially the new person in the room, he would try to promote his vision of where the Croatian borders should be. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he was almost the incorrigible child who wanted the extra scoop of ice-cream and the parents would say: No, I'm sorry, you've had it, that's it. There are the borders, that's it. But even after signing the agreements, there was Tudjman who was, as you've noted, a historian, first and foremost, who had his particular vision of where the Croatian borders should be; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had his particular vision, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But also what I'm trying to get you to admit, because you partially admitted, that you also have David Owen who is representing the EU, who is openly talking with interlocutors, such as Tudjman, that it's okay to look at these international borders and maybe some changes can be made.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me take that, and this is why I've been careful to make the points that I have. First, what David Owen -- the border changes that David Owen proposed were very minor ones and they bore no resemblance to the border changes that Tudjman was suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second, when David Owen was proposing border changes, any of these, he was not representing the EU, and that is why I made the point that these countries supported the Vance-Owen Plan. But David Owen went off on his own, in my view, in proposing these things. I did not feel that that was appropriate. We disagreed with him, and I believe that he set back the peace process by so doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, that's your position and thank you for stating it, but let's be -- let's be -- let's put it into context. David Owen was on the scene well before you got there; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I first went there in December of 1991, so I'm not sure that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you went there on a mission, on a fact-finding mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You went there in 1991 and then you made three trips in 1992. So let's talk about this fact-finding mission. Could you tell us what was the state of the Government of BiH in at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which trip?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At the end of 1992. You've been there 1991 and three times in 1992. Could you tell us in what state it was? Was it a failed state? Was it a state that was fully functioning? Was it a state that could provide services, such as protection for its citizens, paid salaries for teachers, paid salaries for the army, paid salaries for -- have a central bank that's functioning? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I last was there in November of 1992, it was a country that was the victim of brutal aggression. The capital was surrounded by Bosnian Serb army -- soldiers. Snipers were shooting into the capital at innocent people. A large number of mortars were landing. Of course it was extremely difficult for the government to function under those circumstances. That is what happens when countries are victims of aggression. Frankly, the same thing happened in the European countries when the Nazis took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at that point in time, did you have an opportunity to travel around Bosnia and see what the situation was between the Croats and the Muslims during those four trips?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I went to Mostar on one of the trips --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and through some other parts of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in your report that you submitted, what was your analysis or what was your conclusion with respect to what was happening in Central Bosnia or in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only a report that was submitted from one of the trips, and that dealt with the ethnic cleansing of Bosnia-Herzegovina in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the focus of that report on ethnic cleansing, that had to do with the Serbs ethnically cleansing Croats and Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So the focal point of your trip was not to examine the relationship between the Muslims and the Croats and the Serbs, from a political standpoint, but rather -- you're shaking your head. Let me finish my question first. But rather it seems that your trip, at least the first time, was on ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to set this straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first trip, --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which was in December 1991, looked at the overall situation in the former Yugoslavia as the Croatian war was underway, as Slovenia's independence, Croatia independence. The second trip -- and we went to -- in that first trip we went to all the republics and as well as Kosovo. The second trip, which was in August of 1992, was focussed on the Serb-run concentration camps --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get to the third one.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third one was, again, to all the countries that had emerged -- that was in October 1992, that had emerged from the former Yugoslavia, and it dealt with the political situation, broader policy issues. And the fourth trip was with Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan, and it was to Croatia, to Sarajevo, and to Herzegovina, to Mostar, as well as Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during those trips, did you examine the political structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, tracing it from its independence onwards, in order for you to have a picture of how Bosnia and Herzegovina is functioning on a political level? Yes, no, maybe, or I don't recall?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So by this -- and was this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you keep mentioning that Tudjman -- I mean that Izetbegovic was the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would it surprise you to learn that he was the president of the Presidency and not the president of the country? Would that surprise you? And I'll stand on this statement, and I can be corrected later on by the Prosecutor or the Court if I'm misrepresenting the truth.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know how the Presidency functioned? Did you have any idea of how it functioned? Yes, no, maybe, I don't recall?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any idea of how it functioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not going to ask you specifically to tell us, because that might take some time, but let me just put to you: Do you know whether Izetbegovic had more power than the others, being the president of the Presidency? Yes, no, maybe, I don't recall, I don't know? That's the universe of choices.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what if I were to tell you, you are wrong again.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wrong again? When have I been wrong before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you're wrong on this one.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He had no more powers than the others --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, but perhaps you would like me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. I'm going to go through --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you asked if he had more power and I understand fully the legal arrangements, but de facto he had considerably more power than the other members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're going to get to that --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered your question accurately and you said I was wrong, and now you agree I'm right, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're talking about de jure.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I stand corrected. So de facto, even though de jure he's supposed to be the first among equals, de facto the Croats, who were 17.5 per cent of the population, are seeing this Muslim, who is supposed to be first among equals, and saying, No, no, no, I'm on top, it's my government, I'm number one. And in fact the US government is treating him as if, either de jure or de facto, he is the representative of all the people of the entire country. Isn't that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely standard diplomatic practice that the president -- there is one individual who is the head of state, by whatever title he is - president, president of the Presidency Council, what have you - he is the head of state and he's treated that way by the -- by the international community, and it is of the entire country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so let me ask you: In your analysis in these four trips, did you ever prepare a report that would at least set out what functions this government and what functions Izetbegovic, as the president of this country, was able to provide at the local level, at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it not be understandable - and maybe this is a question that's -- that you can't field - but would it not be understandable that the folks at the local level, at the municipal level, should self-organise themselves in order for schools to function, in order, you know, to make sure that salaries are paid, to maybe have some sort of a standing, you know, army, whatever it is, for self-protection? Do you think that's unnatural?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked whether it was understandable --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you by any chance, being a lawyer - I understand you did not practice law, but you did go to Georgetown, which has an excellent curriculum on international courses - did you ever look at the constitution of the former Yugoslavia or of BiH to see whether, to see whether, in the constitution itself it provided for municipalities to self-organise in case of a disaster or in case of an emergency?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I'm going to decline --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to answer a question that is premised on my speaking here as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you did have -- I'm going to slow down. I'm just about ready to -- we have two fine lawyers back there, the "L Department", as I understand that's what the Legal Department is called in the State Department, the "L's". Did you have an "L" in the Croatian embassy -- the American embassy in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't have it. But you had access to lawyers from the State Department. If you wanted some sort of a legal analysis, surely the United States government had enough funds to allow you to make a request to have some lawyer in the State Department, especially at the Balkan Desk, to prepare some sort of an analysis? I mean, assuming that you wanted one. And I'm trying to be fair to the United States government.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United States government is well-resourced in its diplomacy but perhaps not as well-resourced as it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But did you ever ask for a legal opinion to find out what is going on, what sort of structure is being negotiated at the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and thereafter, the Owen-Stoltenberg? So at least you would have some sort of a measuring stick to see -- or was that not part of your mandate and interest since you were in Croatia with instructions towards Tudjman and not concerned about what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina from a political standpoint?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very interested in what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I collected information from all sorts of sources. And, incidentally, these kinds of issues didn't necessarily need a legal analysis from the State Department. There was a very good analysis by the extremely capable legal and constitutional communities in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you by any chance, while you were giving these messages, these demarches to Tudjman, did you ever try to figure out how Herceg-Bosna was set up from, you know, a political -- how it was structured, who was where, how it operated, what competencies it had? Did you ever look at the legislation, either individually or have somebody look at it and give you an analysis?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly looked at the structure of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it was your conclusion that Mate Boban was at the top; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, below him, did you check and see how -- where the responsibilities lie; you know, who was responsible for the military, who was responsible for the civilian government, who was doing what?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have looked at that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it at this point in time you're not in a position - you know, passage of time and what have you - to tell us if I were to ask you concretely to describe it. And I don't think it would be -- I don't want to put you on the spot. But after 13 years, I suspect that you can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I certainly knew more 13 years ago than I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina was functioning; and if so, was it able to circulate currency throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina to the various municipalities, be they Serb, Croat, Muslim-held, or mixed? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know, or I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in this case none of your four choices apply --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because -- for a very important reason, which is that the Bosnian Serbs used their own currency and the Bosnian Croats used the currency of Croatia. That was the Croatian central bank that functioned there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you calculate the time that Mr. Karnavas has used so far. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there a currency for Bosnia and Herzegovina? And was the central bank functioning? Yes, no, maybe? Because -- and I'm asking you the question -- I'll give you a clue here: If it's not functioning, if there's no central bank and there's no currency, then obviously somebody's going to have to do something to get something for buying purposes, paying salaries, and so on and so forth. So my question is very concrete: Was there a central bank? Was it functioning? Was there currency that was widely circulated? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know, or I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: One answer or answers to each of those questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a multiple choice.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I don't remember whether -- at what point the central bank was set up, but certainly because of the aggression it was very hard for it to function. As I recall, certainly in the early period, the effective currency in Bosnia in the government-controlled parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the German mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I understand your answer. Now, I'm going to touch on a few issues, just because I don't have much time. You mentioned in your direct examination that even though it was 17 per cent population, at some point it dropped to 10 per cent because of the issue of allowing citizenship in Croatia. Do you recall that remark?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I said that this was something that Susak and others -- a point Susak and others had made to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the United States government has changed its laws - I have a couple of very talented lawyers here and they'll correct me if I'm wrong - where US citizens can hold a second passport. I'm not talking about a second US passport, because you can't do that. But they can hold -- have a second citizenship and hold a second passport. Is that not a fact? If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. Yes, there are circumstances in which you can be a dual citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the issue of Tudjman allowing Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina to become citizens of Croatia and to hold passports, is it not a fact, sir - and if you don't know, let us know - but is it not a fact that that was offered to every single Croatian no matter where he lived; be he in Cleveland, Ohio, where I come from, or Herceg-Bosna, or Brazil, or whatever. That was an open invitation, because for the first time in modern history, Croatia -- there was an independent, fully independent, Croatian nation.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is: Yes, and it was highly unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it may be highly unusual for us Americans, but maybe --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "unusual" meaning that virtually no other country did it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But the policy wasn't of extending passports in order to draw, you know, and to deplete the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was an unintended consequence and was one of the problems that the Bosnian -- that Croatia and the Bosnian Croats had was the departure of the population --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to Croatia because Croatia was safer and much more prosperous, given the conditions of war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the unintended consequence is also if you're being shelled at and shot at, you're going to get out of the way if you can.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That was one of the unintended consequences. I just wanted to be. That has been an issue, I'm not saying that you're raising, but that has been an issue. Now, you talked about the refugees, so I don't want to go into that. I do want to talk a little bit about foreign fighters. Were you aware at the time that there were foreign fighters in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know, I don't recall?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've testified at length about the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about foreign fighters from Islamic countries?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some of those, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, some of those, and we're going to hear probably from an expert in this court, some of those who came from Islamic countries and were part of the Mujahedin, stayed around and were part of the al-Qaeda. Were you area of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object beyond the scope of the direct examination and beyond the scope of Rule 70. There was no permission from the United States government to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on. I'll move on. We'll get their expert from the Delic case, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever give a demarche to Izetbegovic, you or through the American Ambassador who was in Vienna, apparently, when he should have been in Sarajevo but couldn't because of the Sarajevo government not functioning, but did you ever -- did the US State Department ever send a demarche to Izetbegovic saying: Don't bring in these Mujahedin because they're bad news?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The American Ambassador was in Vienna because the aggression against Sarajevo made it unsafe for him to be in Sarajevo. It was an extremely dangerous situation. And he did make trips there regularly, at considerable risk, as did other internationals who went there, some of whom lost their lives. So I resent the implication of your question about my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he deliver any demarches, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you ought to address the question to him but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You would know. You're talking to him. He's a fellow Ambassador. You're there giving instructions to Tudjman. You're claiming to know what's happening in Central Bosnia. And I'm asking you: Did the State Department that you worked for and you're getting information from as well, did they issue any demarches to Izetbegovic? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm going to object, beyond the scope of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's well within the scope, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no place within the parameters as set by the United States government as attached to the protective measures that allowed examination on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The whole point I'm trying to make is the gentleman here has testified that he knows and knew at the time what was happening in Central Bosnia. He's talking about atrocities, he's talking about all these generalities, and I'm asking him concretely if he knew what was happening on the ground over there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You've asked about the knowledge we had about foreign fighters. I think I answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You now go on to a different matter. I think I could say very clearly, because it's in the Dayton peace treaty, there was obvious US government awareness of the presence of foreign fighters, and one of the provisions of the Dayton peace treaty which we insisted on was the departure of all foreign fighters, and that definitely included the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, but Dayton doesn't come in until 1995, my friend. And, by the way, even after that period, the Mujahedin stayed around, and Holbrooke talks about it in his book. But that's not the point. You're on the scene in 1993. You obviously are aware that the Mujahedin are there. Do either you or your colleague issue a demarche to get those foreign fighters out of there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I've been told that you've already used 57 minutes. It would have been a lot more subtle by asking the witness whether he was aware of any atrocities being committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He would have then said, Yes, and then you could have asked him: In your opinion, who committed the atrocities? And he would have said: X and Y did. And then you could have proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Mr. President, because due to time constraints I'm jumping some steps. But you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So perhaps you could answer Judge Antonetti's questions. Were you aware of atrocities being committed against the Croats by the Muslims? And if so, where, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were atrocities committed by -- by the Bosniaks, by the -- by government forces, and by foreign fighters, the so-called Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know whether you, your colleague, the State Department, Madam Albright, who was at the UN at the time making speeches, talking about the use of force in the region, was there any demarches to Izetbegovic to get those foreign fighters out of there? And, by the way, we have testimony, or we will have testify, that even the local Muslims were afraid of them and wanted them out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to object. Beyond the scope of Rule 70, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is clearly beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in fact that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about -- you touched upon a little bit about the arms shipment during this period of time. And first, I guess I want to go step by step on this, do you recall when the arms embargo was put into place for that region of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN Security Council 713, September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it -- did the US abstain from voting or did they vote for it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bush administration voted for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I know you told us that you're not a lawyer, but you were serving in the diplomatic corps. Do you know whether that resolution was in fact binding law that nations that belonged to the UN had to abide by?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a binding law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it would appear that here -- and I take it, even though the Bush administration voted for it, it was still binding on the Clinton administration as well, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was binding on the United States, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it was binding at the time that you were the Ambassador for the United States to Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it would appear - it would appear - from Holbrooke's book, who was your colleague and is also a fellow democrat, and mentions you in his book in a quite favourable way, by the way, which I'm sure you know - that the arms embargo was being broken basically and the US was aware of it as early as two years before 1994. So it would have been as of 1992 arms were being shipped to Bosnia-Herzegovina with both administrations, the Bush and the Clinton administration, knowing about it. Am I correct or is Mr. Holbrooke correct? It's in footnote 51, by the way, if there's any need.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arms were being shipped to Croatia and to Bosnia, and yes, the United States knew about it. Maybe not all the details, but they knew that at least some arms were going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say -- and in one instance, in fact, President Tudjman comes to you and asks you what should he do since Iran wants to ship weapons through Croatia into Bosnia, to the Muslims in Bosnia, and basically there was wilful blindness - a term of art that we use here sometimes - on the part of the United States and its representative, you, that is, the Ambassador of the United States in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that President Tudjman asked my view on a request -- or asked the view of the United States on a request that was made by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Government of Croatia that arms transit Croatia and go to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in response to that question, I told him that I had no instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's basically -- a wink is as good as a nod, as they say.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in response to that question, I told him I had no instructions. You can draw what inference you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not for me, it's for the Trial Chamber to -- but even before that, you were aware that arms were going to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even though your country, your government, as you put it, had voted for that resolution, you nonetheless did not -- or your government, I should say, because you're not in the position, but your government, did not take a position to stop those arms from going in there.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let us be clear because there's an implication in what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United States did not in any way and at any time, to the best of my knowledge - and I think my knowledge is pretty good - violate the arms embargo. The United States had no obligation to enforce the arms embargo on other countries. Now, that was not a legal obligation as a member of the Security Council. There was also what we considered to be an anomalous situation, that is to say, there were more resolutions that related to the former Yugoslavia than probably any other international problem. And it seemed rather wrong that the only one to be enforced was the arms embargo which imposed -- which enabled the Serbs, who had all the arms, to engage in aggression against Croatia and against Bosnia and Herzegovina, countries that were essentially defenceless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I'll accept that answer, but I posed it because yesterday in a rather, if I might add, regrettably cavalier fashion, you sort of wanted to remind us that Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were living in Croatia at the time should not be going back to their homes to protect their own villages because it was a violation of the law. And so it seems that there is this double standard here. The US can essentially allow weapons to go to the Muslims, but at the same time, here you are as -- telling us that it was wrong for the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina living in -- in the diaspora, which Croatia would have been the diaspora at the time, to go back to protect their own villages, their homes, their loved ones.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're mischaracterising what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that Croatia had an obligation to prevent its citizens from going to a neighbouring country to fight as part of a militia against the lawful against of that country. And I don't think I was cavalier about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. But you don't object -- and then I take it you don't object to individuals who are citizens of both countries, incidentally, from leaving Croatia and going to Bosnia and Herzegovina to fight there? You don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had -- we had a problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, no, you personally. Based on your interpretation of the law, would that be a lawful situation in your book?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United States had a problem with forces that were fighting against the lawful government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And yesterday, at times you characterised the other forces as - and I'm trying to remember the phrase that you used - irregulars. Who were the irregulars? That's what I'm trying to figure out. Who were the irregulars, based on the United States government, which you were representing and you were obviously promoting their position, who did they consider the irregulars? Was it the HVO? Was it these renegade soldiers that you had, as in any war, or individuals behaving in unlawful manners? Who were the irregulars? And I'll limit it. Are you referring to the HVO? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: It was for the lawful authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, the government in -- internationally recognised government in Sarajevo, to determine what were the lawful armed forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And to the extent that the HVO was engaged in war against the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, against the lawful authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was operating in an unlawful way and behaving, if you will, as if it were irregulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me stop you right here and I have one question on that one, and that is: Is it your position that the Army of BiH always acted lawfully against the HVO or against Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's deconstruct that a little bit. If, for instance, units of the ABiH are attacking -- unlawfully are being the aggressors, by your definition, against Croats, is that lawful and is the HVO unlawfully, then, engaging the ABiH, which is being the aggressor, in those instances? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know, too complicated?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose your question is if a lawful armed force is engaged in unlawful activity, do the citizens of a country have the right to engage in [Realtime transcript read in error "re assistance"] resistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess that's one way of putting it, although the HVO was also their citizens, but it was -- by the way, it was - we have testimony here - it was a lawful force.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And just to be clear on the transcript, it's "resistance".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the answer, I think, is -- it's a very good question and I hope you will direct it to someone more learned in these matters than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I just want to -- I don't know when we take our break, but I just want to cover one matter before I sit down and I failed to do so earlier. With respect to the shipment of arms, this issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Judges would like to inform you of the fact that you have run out of time. You have used up far more time than you were granted. We still have Mr. Murphy and perhaps re-examination from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the Coric Defence had 20 minutes remaining, which they have kindly given to our Defence. And with that time, I'm confident that after the break I can conclude my cross-examination, at the latest, by 1.45, possibly before then. So on the basis that we will now take the break and Mr. Karnavas finishes, I don't anticipate any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that Mr. Coric's Defence team gave their 20 minutes to you or to Mr. Karnavas or to no one? I thought it was to no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Tomasegovic Tomic gave me 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. She gave them to you, then. Mr. Scott, would you have any other questions, any additional questions for the witness afterwards? We have to calculate the time we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, under normal circumstances I would. There are a few things, I think in fairness, the Ambassador should have a chance to clarify further. But I'm also very sensitive to the fact that we have to complete this witness by 1.45, and I do not want to hold him over. So, under the circumstances, we are likely to give up our time but I wish we did have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have a couple of minutes, Your Honour. And, incidentally, for the record, Mr. Murphy had passed me a note so I was acting with instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the issue of the arms coming in from Iran was quite a controversial issue. In fact, the republicans, as you know, tried to get some political mileage out of it, if I can put it that way. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct in saying that the republicans tried to get some mileage out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nonetheless it was -- as you testified, it was the reality. And I just want to show you a document, and maybe you could just verify whether this document was shown to you and whether you -- when you testified I believe in a previous case. The number is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for not having it in the e-court. I have a court number. 1C0 -- IC000034. If we could just put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just look at the first page and see whether -- it does have an exhibit number from a previous case. It looks like it's from the Milosevic case. And so I just want to verify whether you are familiar with the document, whether it was shown to you. Is this the document that was presented to you when you testified in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember unless I went back and looked at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that document itself, does it not talk about -- I mean, just by -- if you glean it, if you want to look at -- flip through it, but does it not talk about, in essence, the issue of the shipment of arms from Iran to Bosnia-Herzegovina during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the absence of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you want to hold it and look at it, I mean --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to read it, but it will take me a while to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, just glance through it. Does it in general talk about the issues that we have been talking about, shipments of weapons from Iran to Bosnia during your tenure? I think if you flip through it you'll see the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, frankly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you want to look at it during the break and then tell us whether you recognise it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, in any event, I'll be tendering this document into evidence, Your Honour, and I'll verify that, in just glancing through it, it does talk about the shipments from Iran. It is from the Republican Party, so you can give it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have the break now because it's ten past 12.00. We'll have a 20-minute break and we'll resume at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a document that was shown to the witness before the break. The witness had the opportunity or has had the opportunity of having a look at the document during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I just have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say it was shown to me in the Milosevic case, then I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, it does have an exhibit number, so -- but the contents of the document basically relate to -- and I'm not saying -- I'm not asking you to vouch for the truthfulness of what is contained in the document. But the document itself relates to the issue of shipment of arms from Iran to Bosnia and Herzegovina during the Clinton administration.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last matter, Your Honour. I need to give this a number. It's 1D00917. And with that, that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you very, very much, sir. I appreciate you coming here, and I hope again you will accept my apology when I misspoke and said that you were here to assist the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Mr. Scott, the Defence is requesting that this document be admitted into evidence. Apparently it's a document that was already used, produced, in the Milosevic case. Do you object to having this document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I haven't seen it yet, Your Honour. If I could have a chance to look at it. I thought that the Chamber's ruling was that all the cross-examination material would be provided to the Prosecution, but when we have a chance to look at it, I will come back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Hi. Good afternoon, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: My name is Peter Murphy, and together with my colleague Senka Nozica, we represent Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you had many meetings with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You probably got to know him quite well.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think we could summarise what you said about him by saying that, in a sense, he was a Croatian nationalist.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: When you testified in the Milosevic case - and I can give you the references and show you the transcript if you need it - do you remember that you described him also, though, as being an effective leader?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have described him as an effective leader, and I think you're correct that that came up in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And also, at the same time, you said that he had surrounded himself with some competent advisors.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in that context, you mention Mr. Granic and Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my view, that they were both very competent individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If Mr. Tudjman had the motivation of creating a Greater Croatia, it does not necessarily follow that all his advisors had the same motivation, does it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't think they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it doesn't necessarily follow that everyone in -- that all the Bosnian Croats involved with Herceg-Bosna had any such motivation.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh -- no, no, I don't think that -- I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I understand from your testimony that you consider that to have been an illegal entity.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We considered Herceg-Bosna as a republic to be not a legal entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Well, before that, you are aware, are you not, that when Herceg-Bosna was created, it was originally called not the Republic but the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formally created?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could give you a precise date at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would you accept it from me - and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - that its formal creation was on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think that sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'd like to just go back and draw on your experience, if I can, Ambassador, to recreate a little of what was going on at around that time. By July of 1991, there was war between the -- we can say, the JNA or the Bosnian Serbs on the one hand and Croatia on the other. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think the Bosnian Serbs were involved in it at that time. It was the JNA and the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Quite right. All right. There was a war in which the JNA was involved against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in September of 1991, the United Nations imposed the arms embargo on the whole of the former Yugoslavia, did it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I don't want to go over your testimony again on that. You very fairly agreed, I think, that that was an embargo effectively against everybody except the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know when the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the United States?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give the precise date, but it was around -- it was April or May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would you agree, about the 6th, 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that sounds right, the same day as the recognition of Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, actually, wasn't Croatia recognised a little earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Might have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In January --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a couple days before. Not by the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: By the European Union, then?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that, accepting that the Community of Herceg-Bosna was created in November 1991, that was before the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you were asked in examination-in-chief - and we can look at the documents if you wish; I don't think it's necessary - but about a meeting that you attended with President Tudjman in October 1993 where he had misquoted the French and German Ambassadors as saying that there was a general belief that Bosnia and Herzegovina could not survive. Do you remember -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would you not agree with me that in the summer of 1991, going back now some two years before that, the question of whether Bosnia and Herzegovina could survive was a very real question?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, insofar as a war followed, the answer to that is yes. But at that time, the focus of the international community was primarily on Slovenia and Croatia and the war that was brewing in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But that war was being conducted, at least in part, using the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a springboard from which to attack Croatia. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But I think it's important to remember, at one point the headquarters for the UN operation for Croatia was going to be put in Sarajevo on the grounds that it was safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it turned out not to be quite true.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international community ought to have recognised that the survival of Bosnia was at risk, but it didn't. And I think we could -- I could cite a lot of evidence that -- of where they -- where there were oversights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm just pausing for the French translation, Ambassador. Certainly by the beginning of 1992, the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina was clearly a question in the mind of the international community, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the -- well, I think it was a matter of growing concern. Obviously by April it was page 1 news.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you not agree with me that between November of 1991 and really up to the signing of the Dayton Peace Treaty. There was not really a time when the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was effectively in control of its entire territory?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I think you agreed today in questioning by one of my colleagues that the -- the very operation of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout that period was extremely difficult because of the wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in November 1991, if one thinks of it from the position of the Bosnian Croats, let's say those in Herzegovina, would you not agree, sir, that there was every reason for them to be afraid for their political and social future?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And indeed, you've already told us that you wrote a report in August of 1992 detailing the ethnic cleansing by the Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You testified in the Milosevic case - and again, I can give you the reference - that it was your opinion that Milosevic was trying to create a Greater Serbia in alliance with the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think you testified that his territorial ambitions included, if not the whole, certainly a very great part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also some of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I so testified in that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You also testified, did you not, that, even when it became clear in 1993 that the goal of Greater Serbia was really effectively impossible, Milosevic still, nonetheless, harboured some very extensive territorial ambitions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Again, at the expense of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You also testified I think in that same trial that during 1992 the -- the JNA, which later became the VRS, and also Serb paramilitaries were more or less operating at will in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And today you said that -- I don't want to go back; we had an extensive discussion. But I think you agreed that for various reasons including the 1992 presidential election, perhaps the United States did not take the most effective action that could have been taken to prevent that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, again if I could draw your experience and knowledge for one other matter relating to the Community of Herceg-Bosna. In the spring of 1991, so this is now some time before Herceg-Bosna, the Serb political party, the SDS, began to form communities of municipalities, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: One such community was established in the Bosnian Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And by the fall of 1991, those communities had been transformed into what became known as the Serbian Autonomous Districts or SAOs?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is it also true that in October 1991 the -- the Bosnian Serbs established their own independent assembly, round about that time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the dates, but I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'll be corrected if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So if you would accept that. And -- and then one other date on the same basis, if we could, that the SDS also in November of 1991, on the 9th and 10th, held a plebiscite as to whether they wished to remain in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And so, I know I've painted for you a -- tried to paint something of a picture of what was going on at that time, but we can assume that when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established in November of 1991, it was established against that general political background?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: As far as the issue of the legality of entities goes, do you make any distinction between the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the later Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it might be easier and quicker if I explain what it was that we considered to be illegal. We considered to be -- or not legal. We considered the to be not legal to have an entity exercising, or seeking to exercise, sovereign governmental functions with its own armed forces engaged again in armed conflict against the internationally recognised government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And therefore, to the extent that the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna evolved into such an entity, it then met the threshold conditions that -- that led to my characterisation of it as being not legal. And certainly also, to add, that it continued after there was an agreement to dissolve it was also, of course, a sense that it was not legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So then if I'm understanding then correctly, Ambassador, your characterisation of it as being illegal is much more concerned with military activities against the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina rather than simply its existence?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly its -- as I said, its exercise of sovereign governmental powers, including most importantly military powers not under the control of the sovereign government and, indeed even worse, against the control of the internationally recognised government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in rendering that opinion, again you've taken into account, have you, the fact that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was in fact established before the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you testified at length during examination-in-chief- and I don't want to go through it all, so let me summarise and then you can tell me if I summarise inaccurately. It was your view that the Republic of Croatia was supporting, sponsoring, and directing the HVO of Herceg-Bosna. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Substantially correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, did you not testify in so many words that President Tudjman was the de facto president and commander-in-chief of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did so testify, and that was my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that Mr. Susak was the de facto minister of defence of the HVO as well as the minister of defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did testify to that, and that is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that whenever the -- you as the United States Ambassador wanted, as you put it, action, you would go always to Zagreb to get the action that you required?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The address that produced results from the HVO was the leadership in Zagreb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Does it not follow then from your testimony, Ambassador, that to the extent there were people, Bosnian Croats, purporting to hold administrative or governmental offices in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, that these people in your view were simply puppets of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll stay away from the characterisation of puppets, but stick with my testimony, which is that the Government of Croatia exercised substantial control over the HVO and the governmental authorities of the Bosnian Croat community in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, now you're saying "substantial control" or I heard the French translation, "controle essentiel"; that is now your characterisation of the relationship?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used the word "puppet" which I don't think is a word I used. I think as I presented it in the examination-in-chief is how I meant it, and the simplest way to do it is to say that in my view President Tudjman was the de facto president of Herceg-Bosna and Gojko Susak was the de facto defence minister, with all that that implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
