utterances.text: You said in response to Mr. Karnavas that at the time you were, to some extent, familiar with the various legislative acts of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the legislation that they passed?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said was that I was familiar with some of the -- some of the structure, organisational structure, and I suppose some of the legislation of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Have you ever met William Tomljanovich? He's a research officer employed by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, have you -- did you meet with him for the purpose of discussing this case or your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with the researchers of the OTP, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you whether Mr. Tomljanovich was one of the people that you met with.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was you would have met with him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've met with the OTP so many times on these cases that it's frankly a little hard for me to be precise, and I apologise to the Court. I mean, the fact is that I've been doing many other things in the years since I've left Croatia. I think the first meetings were back in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I quite understand, Ambassador. You -- but I think the last time you testified here was in Milosevic, that would have been in 2003, is it --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was in Martic in April of 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. But in relation to this case, which a case involving Bosnian Croats as opposed to Serbs, you don't remember specifically, just in a rough time-frame, when you've met with the --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've met with them at different times. I've met with them in the State Department in the 1990s. I've met a number of times with them -- well, let's see, I met in -- when, I think, I was here for the Martic case I met with them. I met with them in December of 2005 when I came to testify in a -- in The Hague in a Dutch war crimes case relating to Iraq. I met with them at the time of the Milosevic case. I mean, I've had -- and the -- I think there have been other encounters. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine. Not within the last month or so anyway?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Not within the last month or so anyway?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I met with the OTP within the last month, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. You've not had the opportunity to read a report that Mr. Tomljanovich prepared for the purposes of this case, have you, dealing with the governmental structure of the Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you take any steps before coming to give evidence in this case to refresh your memory about the general organisation or structure of the Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, just let me ask you in general terms then: Are you aware that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna set up a -- what we could call an administrative structure?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That they took steps to deal with social and political matters such as crime prevention?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That they set up a commission, more than one commission, to investigate war crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I remember that specifically, but the parties to the conflict did have commissions to investigate war crimes which invariably meant crimes committed by the other side and not by their own side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that they established a system of courts and adopted a criminal code?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That they made provisions to deal with issues affecting refugees?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And for the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure they made provisions for the exchange of prisoners, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Ambassador, do you -- by the way, I meant to ask you, do you speak or read Croatian?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at least in a very, very primitive level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Were you aware ever of the publication by the Community of Herceg-Bosna the Official Gazette, the Narodni List?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In view of everything that we have discussed, would you acknowledge the possibility that the creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had at least something to do with defensive measures against the Serbian threat, as opposed to some territorial ambition in the mind of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would you acknowledge the possibility that there were other driving forces behind the administration of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna other than President Tudjman's obsession with the borders of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. As you have described, the Herceg-Bosna formed -- performed many governmental functions and so it was not just about President Tudjman's territorial ambitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Ambassador, with the assistance of the usher, could we please see on e-court a Prosecution exhibit that you were shown previously during examination-in-chief, the number is P09504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, that is a document under seal. We shall have to go into private session unless the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: This is a cable sent from the Zagreb embassy in October 1993, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct -- sorry, would you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: This is a cable sent from the embassy in Zagreb during -- during August 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in fact, in this cable you were reporting on a visit by officers of the embassy at your direction to the Heliodrom. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If we could focus at the top of the page thereon, the paragraph headed "summary." Mr. Scott directed your attention to certain passages of this. I don't want to go back over them all, but probably due to lack of time he didn't read all of them. I'd just like to refer to one or two others. About four lines down there in that paragraph does it -- do you report back: "But the officers were allowed unrestricted access to buildings throughout the facility"? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to have the record clear, the full sentence is: "The camp officials prohibited private conversations with prisoners, but the officers were allowed unrestricted access to buildings throughout the facility."

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I understand, I was avoiding repeating -- Mr. Scott, I think for a lack of time, probably omitted the second part of that sentence. I just wanted to bring it out. Would you also read the next sentence aloud for us, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In general, the prisoners looked okay, were being fed, and had access to medical care."

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to, if we could -- I'm not sure quite what page this would be on e-court. Do I give you an R number for that? What's the most helpful way to do it? I want to go to the paragraph called "food and medical care." It should be about two pages further on in the English version. Yes, thank you. The paragraph -- if we could bring that up. Thank you very much. Do you see there, Ambassador, the paragraph headed "food and medical care"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And five lines up from the end of that paragraph let me read it to you. "The embassy team visited a well-stocked medical clinic and were told by the doctor on duty that he cared for not only prisoners but also for civilians who were no longer able to get to Mostar because of the fighting." Again, that was something else that was reported to you by the officers that you sent to inspect?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And then finally, if we could go to the next page under the heading "overall assessment." Thank you. If we could bring that paragraph into focus. And again, omitting passages that were read to you before, five lines down you see a sentence beginning: "The number of 1400 prisoners ..."?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it continues: "The number of 1400 prisoners given by the commander was consistent with what the officers saw, although an exact figure requires a formal census." And then the next sentence reads: "Conditions appeared to be generally acceptable with no overt signs of maltreatment or malnutrition." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, I bear in mind all of the other passages in that report that Mr. Scott read to you. But the passages that I have read to you were -- they reflect accurately the report that you were given by the officers that you sent to make the inspection?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to be as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have a moment to confer with Ms. Nozica. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I've concluded my cross-examination, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy. Mr. Scott, we have some time left if you have any re-examination. A little earlier on you were complaining about perhaps not having the possibility of putting additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have to say, Your Honour, in all candour, I did not expect to have time and certainly not this much time, but I appreciate Mr. Murphy's efficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions, Ambassador. We've talked a number of things, and would you agree that when we were talking about events in the former Yugoslavia, it's quite important on most occasions to talk about specific dates and specific places?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you confirm to the Judges, if you know, is it true that there were between 1991 and 1995, until Dayton, that there were many times and many places in Bosnia and Herzegovina where both the Croats and Muslims fought together against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Any come to mind?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they fought together in 1992. They fought together in the defence of Sarajevo. In fact, they fought together in some of the events that have been discussed today, including the liberation of Mostar. It has to be recalled, actually, that Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims were a significant component of the HVO until the Muslim-Croat war started. And then after the Washington Agreement, there came again an effective military alliance between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian government. And just to be completely clear, because I think there may having some ambiguity, it was at that time, after the Muslim-Croat war was over, that I had the conversation that I discussed with Mr. Prlic's counsel about -- and which I said to President Tudjman that we had no -- we had no -- I had no instructions on the matter of weapons that were going into Bosnia. But anyhow, subsequent to that there was close cooperation. And then in 1995 - and I think this is very important - the Bosnian government requested the assistance of the Croatian army in a military offensive that -- it went up the Livno Valley. This was after the fall of Srebrenica, at a meeting in Split between Presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic. In fact, I was at that meeting. They made -- the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina made a lawful request and the -- for military assistance, and the Government of Croatia accepted, and the end result was a military campaign that changed the balance and created conditions that led us directly to Dayton just a few months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There has been evidence in the case, and in fact your testimony, I believe, on the first day, that the Croat population of Bosnia-Herzegovina at some time is estimated around 17, 17 and a half per cent, and in your view possibly quite smaller than that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 17 per cent in the 1991 census. But what -- it wasn't my personal view, it was the view of the Croatian officials who were most knowledgeable about Bosnia, notably Defence Minister Susak, that the population had fallen to 12 to 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Given that situation, Ambassador, can you tell the Judges, did the Croats, the Croats in Croatia or the Croats in Bosnia, could they have any hope of defeating or overcoming or evicting the Serbs without Muslim participation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection on the grounds that there is -- first of all, it goes beyond the scope, but even if it is within the scope of cross-examination, there needs to be a foundation laid if the gentleman is capable of answering that particular question. So if he wishes, if it is within the scope, I would ask that some foundation be laid for the gentleman to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we just have, Your Honour. We talked about the demographics and the amount of the population, and therefore the manpower that these various forces had to draw on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, let me remind my colleague here that the Ambassador at the time never visited Central Bosnia, nor has he testified that he was familiar with the various capabilities of the various units in Central Bosnia. So unless we can have some sort of a foundation, I think now we're going into areas where perhaps we don't have sufficient knowledge that this gentleman has the knowledge and capabilities of answering that question without speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the Defence questioning apparently everyone thought that Mr. Galbraith had sufficient knowledge and basis to talk about everything and repeatedly put questions to him about a wide range of subjects in dealing -- including military matters. It was the Ambassador himself who said -- raised this issue of population and has talked many times, as he just did a few moments ago, about Serb -- about the Muslim-Croat cooperation in various respects. This question follows directly from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here's why I object to this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we make a decision. Mr. Scott, rephrase your question so that we can clearly see its relevance and direct link to the cross-examination. What is the exact question that you would like to pose?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The question is: Could the Croats have had any hope of defeating the Serbs without the participation of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, where, in what place are we talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In Bosnia between 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Bosnia is a big country and there was war between -- Muslim against Muslim, Serbs against Croats, Serbs against Muslim, Croats -- I mean, where are we talking about? What area? The Posavina? Central Bosnia? Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're talking about the war in Bosnia, as we have been all day today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why is this relevant, Your Honour? And again, I stress it's beyond the scope and also there's no foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what is the relevance of the question you want to ask? How does it relate to the indictment and what is it that you would like to demonstrate by the answer that the witness might give? Because the question you have asked concerns hypothetical events -- or rather, it's a hypothetical question and concerns a period before he assumed his position as Ambassador. If he answers your question, it's because he had certain prior knowledge about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you've asked me several questions. The relevance of the question is -- I believe that there's -- the suggestion might be -- I submit to you, the suggestion may be in the future there was something inconsistent with the fact that arms and military equipment were sometimes being sent through Croatia to the Muslim forces. Now, an explanation -- one of the explanations for that is because indeed the Muslims were fighting together against the Serbs. That's one point of relevance. It also may be represented and suggested at times what Mr. Tudjman's -- President Tudjman's ambitions or thoughts were on this matter. And I want to give the Ambassador the chance to respond that it was a very complex situation in which Tudjman had to calculate a number of different factors, including the fact that sending arms into Bosnia was necessary to defeat the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have decided that you may ask the question, having considered the objection. Ambassador, could you answer Mr. Scott's question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is -- I need to take the question in parts. By themselves and supported by Croatia financially and with arms, the Bosnian Croats had no chance of defeating the Serbs. So it was essential to have an alliance with the Bosnian Muslims. Croatia itself deploying the army that it had in 1995 might have been able to defeat the -- obviously it did defeat the Croatian Serbs easily and it might have been able to defeat the Bosnian Serbs on its own. But it was certainly -- I mean, we can't tell that. And certainly it was very much a joint effort. I think there's another factor here, though, that's very important. One talks about the fact that the United States and, incidentally, not just the United States, Germany, France, Britain, all the major countries knew that arms were going both to Croatia and to Bosnia and Herzegovina and -- and all chose to look the other way, to turn, if you will, a blind eye. The only difference between the United States and those other countries is that the United States was asked by the president of Croatia and declined to answer. I said I had no instructions. Now, I say this because had there -- the Muslim-Croat war not ended, it is very likely, indeed close to certain, that there would have been sanctions on Croatia that would have effectively cut off the much, much larger flow of arms to Croatia and, in turn then, Croatia could not have recovered its own territory or helped change the military balance in Bosnia. So the -- Croatia had itself very strong reasons related to the territorial integrity of Croatia itself to end the Muslim war -- Muslim-Croat war and to support a military alliance with the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I appreciate -- I appreciate the statements from the Ambassador and I just want to remind the Trial Chamber that we're not in front of some senate subcommittee hearing, you know, where we need to repeat the mantra of the day. I think we've established that there was a joint criminal enterprise to violate the embargo; we've just verified it. But beyond that, I would ask that the answers be restricted to the questions posed. I appreciate all the other commentary. We've heard it. We appreciate the Ambassador's position, which was the United States position at the time. But I think that once too many we're at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this commentary of Mr. Karnavas is completely inappropriate. It is nothing more than his just getting up and making a speech, as so often happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, Ambassador. You were quite direct in pointing out that in various respects the Republic of Croatia had, for instance, assisted the refugees in the former Yugoslavia to a great degree and had done certain things, let's put it, supporting refugees, supporting humanitarian aid at various times. And you pointed this out in your cross-examination I think mostly yesterday. I want to give you the opportunity - and I think the case that should be put to you because the suggestion may be made at some time in the future after you have left - the Defence case would be that because of what you have said that is inconsistent with President Tudjman, Susak, and others having this Greater Croatia objective. So I'd like to give you the opportunity to explain to the Judges how you reconcile or to explain both of those things.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no inconsistency at all. First, I think there was a genuine humanitarian impulse on the part of the Croatian leaders. Mate Ganic, I believe, cared personally and deeply about refugees. I think the people of Croatia represent a liberal and humanitarian society. There was enormous public sympathy in Croatia for the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember during one of my visits in the main square in Zagreb, there was a flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and people went there to light candles. So frankly Croatia's humanitarian role reflected the goodness of Croatian society. And frankly -- and I also have testified, but I will repeat, the ambitions for Greater Croatia was held by a limited number of people. Frankly, most Croatians weren't all that fond of the Herzegovinians and they were not looking to annex this particular territory, but there was a small group, certainly including Tudjman and certainly including Susak, that did desire a Greater Croatia. Incidentally, I think both Tudjman and Susak were supportive of humanitarian measures. So that they had these ambitions doesn't mean that everything they did was wrong. And beyond that, there was of course a very practical consideration. Croatia needed the support of the West, and one of its biggest political cards, probably its biggest political card, both with Europe and the United States, was its role in taking care of refugees and in making possible humanitarian assistance. And that, in fact, was a very important reason why we were -- why we were reluctant to impose sanctions on Croatia, why it was a difficult decision. Not because we expected Croatia to retaliate against the refugees, but because it would make life for Croatia more difficult and limit its ability to carry out this important humanitarian mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the Judges has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have testified about crimes and violations of human rights in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period that we are interested in. And when Mr. Murphy showed you P09504, we saw that your telegram made reference to detainees who had been treated correctly, they had been provided with adequate medical care, et cetera. My question is: What is your personal conclusion with regard to the detention of these individuals? We're talking about October 1993. What is your conclusion with regard to the detention of individuals at the Heliodrom? And in general, what conclusion do you draw with regard to the detention of the individuals in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in general, individuals were held in appalling conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course the worst offenders were the Bosnian Serbs. The HVO-run camps, I think, varied at -- depending on the camp and depending on the time. And of course we got access at a time when, because of our pressure, conditions had improved and also where the commanders knew that the American embassy was coming to visit. So they -- you know, they had some opportunity to clean things up, and they also did not allow interviews with the prisoners. But the short answer is that in some cases the conditions were appalling with some beatings, summary execution, lack of sanitary conditions, rapes. In some cases they were better, but I would note that even in the Heliodrom one of the issues was the -- was forced labour on the front lines, exposing prisoners to the danger of being killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reviewing my notes, Mr. Ambassador, I have no further questions for you. And I thank you once again for your testimony and assistance.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question that relates to the question put to you by my colleague. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an ambassador in Zagreb, I assume that you have a press service, television, radios, you have sources of information while you were in that position. In the second part of 1993, in particular, did you receive via the media information about what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was there a flow of information, as is now the case in Iraq and elsewhere, the CNN coverage, there's a lot of information one receives in real time, in particular the case with regard to the events in Beirut. At the time that you were there, did you have information as being evidence according to which journalists were in the field, there were reports for sure. Did you obtain information through the media, and I'm not referring to your tradition sources of information, but did you gain information through the media that allowed you to gain a picture of events that were actually unfolding there?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course we had all sources of information. I have to tell you that in fact the media is some of the most important sources of information. I think for those who are not in government, there's the impression that -- that secret sources must be extremely valuable. But the truth is that probably the most important information comes from public sources and in -- and the media was hugely important. There was, of course, the local media, and if you watched the television of different parties and listened to the radio you got some different pictures. But the international press did absolutely heroic work in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They brought this war home, not just to me who was living in the region and therefore living with it, but to the policy-makers in Europe and America. And every day they, in their offices and at dinnertime, they were reminded of what was happening in Sarajevo, Mostar, and in Omarska, and so on. And so it was a hugely important source of information and it did provide the big picture. The other advantage that I had personally was that most journalists would pass through Zagreb on their way in and out of Bosnia, and they would come by to see me. So not only did I have the benefit of what they wrote or what they showed on television, but I also had the benefit of talking to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on the basis of the information you obtained from the media, on the basis of what you could see on television, on the basis of what you could learn from journalists, were you able to contact President Tudjman and to draw his attention to the events that the international community could witness through the -- through the media? Was it possible for you to tell him that it was perhaps necessary to act on that basis?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- the answer is yes, and in two ways. First, I could -- I could and did take to him reports that appeared in the international media. But secondly, I sent messages to him through the -- my interviews with Croatian newspapers, magazines, and on Croatian television. And frankly, everything that I have described -- or almost everything that I have described here in the -- in the demarches that I made to Tudjman personally are also messages that I delivered publicly to the Croatian media. I said very clearly that -- for example, that we held Croatia responsible for the conduct of the HVO and that if that conduct did not improve there would be sanctions on Croatia. I warned publicly about the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it was -- it was a very -- the media was a very important part of our diplomacy and a way to send messages and, frankly, to build support among the Croatian people, most of whom, as I've testified, in my view did not support the policies of Tudjman with regard to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this concludes your examination, your testimony. On behalf of the Judges, I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague. This isn't the first time you have come here, but I hope that it will be the last time because you can't spend your life testifying before Judges. I would like to thank you, and I would also like to thank the representatives of the US Government who have been present during the testimony. I wish you a safe return home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you and the representatives of the US Government out of the court-room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few more minutes. I'll give the floor to both parties so that we can have the exhibit numbers. We'll be able to make good use of the time in this way. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The Prosecution tenders as through this witness -- through this witness Exhibits P05047, P06251. P09502. P09503, P09504, P09505, P09506, P09507, P05104, P09508, P09498, P09499, P03240, P05090, P06412, P09501, P09500, P09697, P03673, P05047, P07789, P09510, and P07475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I now turn to Defence counsel in the order you wish to follow. Perhaps we'll start with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. President, I just had that one document, which I believe it's 1D00917, and I understand the Prosecution wanted to at least double-check and make sure that that was a document from the Milosevic case, but -- it has an exhibit from that case. But in any event that's the only document that we showed and tendered in this case -- in this -- for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Stojic Defence has no documents to tender through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have prepared the documents we used, but I must add a reservation; I can correct myself later on. We also used some documents that have already been admitted, but I have not marked these. I think that can easily be amended afterwards. We wish to tender document 3D00141, 3D00320, 3D00375, 3D00376, 3D00377, 3D00186, 3D00299, 3D00378, that's the document that was on the ELMO and in the meantime it has been assigned a number and put into e-court. Of the Prosecutor's exhibits, I wish to tender - and I have no objection to their having a P number - is P9601, P6251, and P3112. These are the documents used by myself and General Praljak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have only one document to tender. This is Ambassador Galbraith's interview published in Globus 4D00326. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will render our decision, having checked the numbers of all these documents. We have two minutes remaining. My attention has been drawn to the application of Rule 89(F) that concerns witnesses because I have been informed that the Prosecution also intends to tender documents into evidence. As there will be no examination-in-chief, it would be good, Mr. Scott, if one showed these documents to the witness by the e-court system. You can then say: I'm showing you such and such a document, 1, 2, 3, 4, et cetera, do you recognise them? And then the witness will say: Yes, I recognise them, I have seen them already. Is that what you intended to do? Is that how you intended to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate the Court's clarification. I think there's been some misunderstanding about that. With many of these witnesses, the Rule 89(F) procedure will be that -- of course, the witness will be brought into the court-room, they will be given a chance to look at their prior statement to confirm that that indeed would be their testimony. It may be that the Prosecution might ask them a few questions to clarify or highlight a particular part of their testimony and that any documents to be tendered through the witness would be examined with the witness. So I think it was a bit of a misunderstanding. It could happen in some cases or a simplification to think that there would be nothing more than simply a standing up and tendering the written statement. The written statement will be the vast majority of the testimony of the witnesses, supplemented by -- primarily in connection with documents. So, yes, we do intend to take the witness through any exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll deal with that as things unfold. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one request. On the 7th of September we received in French a decision on adjudicated facts. As, unfortunately, we are not so conversant with French, to see whether there are any grounds for appeal, we wish to ask for your leave to discuss this decision on receipt of the English text and then perhaps lodge an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's not a problem. You may always make a request for an appeal, but it's the Chamber that shall decide. It's quarter to 2.00. I wish you a good weekend. Those who are now ill, well, I hope they will soon be in good health again so that they can all be here on Monday. I'll see you next Monday then.
